anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: Which nerve is injured by a fracture at the surgical neck of the humerus, and what is the classic mechanism?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: The axillary nerve (C5–C6). Also injured by anterior shoulder dislocation.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: What motor and sensory deficit results from an axillary nerve injury?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: Motor: deltoid (abduction 15–90°) and teres minor. Sensory: the “regimental badge” area over the lateral shoulder.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: Which nerve runs in the spiral (radial) groove and is injured by a midshaft humeral fracture?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: The radial nerve — producing wrist drop. Also compressed in “Saturday night palsy”.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: What is the motor and sensory loss with a radial nerve injury?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: Motor: wrist & finger extensors, supinator, triceps → wrist drop. Sensory: dorsal 1st web space.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: Where are the two classic sites of median nerve injury?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: The carpal tunnel (wrist) and a supracondylar fracture (elbow).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: What muscles does the median nerve supply in the hand (mnemonic)?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: LOAF: Lateral 2 lumbricals, Opponens pollicis, Abductor pollicis brevis, Flexor pollicis brevis (plus most forearm flexors).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: What is the sensory territory of the median nerve in the hand?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: The lateral (radial) 3½ fingers on the palmar side.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: Where are the two classic sites of ulnar nerve injury?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: Behind the medial epicondyle / cubital tunnel (elbow) and Guyon’s canal (wrist, between pisiform & hook of hamate).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: What does the ulnar nerve supply in the hand?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: The intrinsic muscles: interossei, hypothenar muscles, medial 2 lumbricals and adductor pollicis. Sensory: medial 1½ fingers.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: Which nerve supplies serratus anterior and what deformity follows its injury?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: The long thoracic nerve (C5–C7) → winged scapula. Classic cause: axillary node clearance / mastectomy.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: What is the “hand of benediction” — which nerve and when is it seen?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: A median nerve lesion: on trying to make a fist the index & middle fingers can’t flex and stay pointing (a high lesion).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: What is the “ape hand” deformity?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: A median nerve sign at rest: thenar wasting with the thumb pulled into the plane of the palm (lost opposition & abduction).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: Describe the ulnar claw hand.
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: Ring & little fingers hyperextended at the MCP joints and flexed at the IP joints — loss of the medial 2 lumbricals/interossei with unopposed long flexors/extensors.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: What is the ulnar paradox?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: A higher (elbow) ulnar lesion produces a less obvious claw, because the medial half of FDP is also paralysed so the fingertips can’t curl. The claw worsens with a distal lesion or as a proximal one recovers.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: What is Froment’s sign and what does it test?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: To hold paper between thumb & index the patient flexes FPL (median) to compensate for a weak adductor pollicis (ulnar) — a sign of ulnar nerve palsy.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: What are the roots, mechanism and posture of Erb’s palsy?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: C5–C6 (upper trunk). Excess head–shoulder separation (shoulder dystocia / fall on shoulder). Posture: adducted, internally rotated, extended elbow, pronated forearm = “waiter’s tip”.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: What are the roots and features of Klumpke’s palsy?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: C8–T1 (lower trunk). Loss of the hand intrinsics → claw hand; may injure T1 sympathetics → Horner’s syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: Give the order of the brachial plexus from proximal to distal.
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: Roots → Trunks → Divisions → Cords → Branches (“Randy Travis Drinks Cold Beer”). Roots C5–T1; cords named by their relation to the axillary artery.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: A midshaft clavicle fracture: what is the commonest site and what pulls the medial fragment up?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: The middle third is commonest; the medial fragment is elevated by sternocleidomastoid.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: Why does a proximal-pole scaphoid fracture risk avascular necrosis and non-union?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: Its blood supply enters distally (dorsal carpal branch of the radial artery) and runs retrograde, so a proximal fracture starves the proximal fragment.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: How should you manage a FOOSH with anatomical snuffbox tenderness but a normal X-ray?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: Treat as a scaphoid fracture: immobilise in a thumb spica and re-image (repeat X-ray or MRI) in 10–14 days — never discharge as a sprain.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: What are the borders and floor of the anatomical snuffbox?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: Borders: EPL (ulnar side); APL + EPB (radial side). Floor: scaphoid & trapezium. The radial artery crosses it.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: Distinguish a Colles’ from a Smith’s fracture.
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: Colles’ = distal radius with dorsal angulation (“dinner-fork”), FOOSH in the elderly. Smith’s = volar angulation (“reverse Colles’”), fall on a flexed wrist.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: What passes through the carpal tunnel?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: 9 flexor tendons (4 FDS, 4 FDP, 1 FPL) plus the median nerve, deep to the flexor retinaculum.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: Why is thenar skin sensation spared in carpal tunnel syndrome?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve arises before the tunnel and runs superficial to the retinaculum, so it is not compressed (though the thenar muscles waste).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: Name two bedside tests for carpal tunnel syndrome.
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: Tinel’s sign (tapping over the nerve) and Phalen’s test (sustained wrist flexion) reproduce the paraesthesia.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: What are the four rotator cuff muscles and which is most commonly torn?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: SITS: Supraspinatus (initiates abduction 0–15°, most commonly torn), Infraspinatus & teres minor (external rotation), Subscapularis (internal rotation).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: What is the commonest direction of shoulder dislocation and which nerve must you check?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: Anterior (~95%). Document axillary nerve function (regimental-badge sensation & deltoid) before and after reduction.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: What are the contents of the cubital fossa (lateral → medial)?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: TAN: biceps Tendon · brachial Artery · median Nerve. The median cubital vein crosses the roof (venepuncture site).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: What are the “6 Ps” of compartment syndrome and the key management point?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: Pain (out of proportion & on passive stretch — earliest), Paraesthesia, Pallor, Pulselessness (late), Paralysis, Perishingly cold. Treat with emergency fasciotomy — don’t wait for a lost pulse.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: What is Volkmann’s ischaemic contracture and its classic cause?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: A fixed flexion contracture of the wrist & fingers from untreated forearm compartment syndrome — classically after a supracondylar fracture injuring the brachial artery.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.front: How are axillary lymph nodes grouped, and what do they drain?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.back: Levels I–III relative to pectoralis minor (I below, II behind, III above). They drain the upper limb and ~75% of the breast — key in breast cancer staging.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: The upper limb divides into compartments — what nerve and overall action define the anterior arm?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: Musculocutaneous nerve (C5–C7). It flexes the elbow & shoulder and supinates the forearm.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: What nerve and action define the posterior arm compartment?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: Radial nerve (C5–T1). It extends the elbow.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: What nerve and action define the anterior forearm compartment?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: Median nerve (with 1½ ulnar exceptions). It flexes the wrist/fingers and pronates.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: What nerve and action define the posterior forearm compartment?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: Radial nerve — the deep muscles via its continuation the posterior interosseous nerve (PIN). It extends the wrist/fingers and supinates.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: Which 1½ muscles of the anterior forearm are supplied by the ulnar (not median) nerve?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: Flexor carpi ulnaris + the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: State the golden rule linking compartment position to action throughout the limb.
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: Anterior = flexor; posterior = extensor — true for both the arm and the forearm.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: What is the nerve and action of serratus anterior, and the consequence of its palsy?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: Long thoracic nerve; it protracts the scapula and rotates it upward. Palsy → winged scapula and inability to abduct >90°.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: What is the nerve supply of trapezius?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: The accessory nerve (CN XI) (with proprioceptive C3–C4).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: Give the actions and nerve of latissimus dorsi.
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: Extends, adducts & medially rotates the arm; thoracodorsal nerve. (“The handcuff / swimmer’s muscle”.)

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: What is the nerve and action of the rhomboids?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: Dorsal scapular nerve; they retract and downwardly rotate the scapula.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: Which two muscles form the force couple that upwardly rotates the scapula for overhead abduction?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: Trapezius (upper + lower fibres) and serratus anterior.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: What is the nerve and main action of the deltoid?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: Axillary nerve; the main abductor from 15–90° (anterior fibres flex/medially rotate, posterior fibres extend/laterally rotate).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: Name the four rotator cuff muscles (“SITS”).
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: Supraspinatus, Infraspinatus, Teres minor, Subscapularis.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: What is the action and nerve of supraspinatus?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: Initiates abduction (0–15°); suprascapular nerve. It is the most commonly torn cuff muscle.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: Which rotator cuff muscles laterally rotate the shoulder?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: Infraspinatus and teres minor.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: Which rotator cuff muscle medially rotates the shoulder?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: Subscapularis (the only anterior cuff muscle).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: What is the overall functional role of the rotator cuff?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: The dynamic stabilisers that hold the humeral head in the shallow glenoid fossa during movement.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: Describe the abduction sequence and the muscle responsible for each phase.
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: 0–15° supraspinatus → 15–90° deltoid → 90–180° scapular upward rotation (trapezius + serratus anterior).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: Name the prime movers of shoulder flexion.
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: Anterior deltoid and pectoralis major (clavicular head) are the prime movers; coracobrachialis and biceps assist.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: Name the prime movers of shoulder extension.
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: Latissimus dorsi, teres major, posterior deltoid.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: What is the strongest action of biceps brachii, and when is it maximal?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: Supination of the forearm — maximal when the elbow is flexed. (It also flexes the elbow.)

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: Give the origins of the two heads of biceps brachii.
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: Long head — supraglenoid tubercle; short head — coracoid process. Inserts on the radial tuberosity.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: Which muscle is the workhorse elbow flexor (flexes in every position) and where does it insert?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: Brachialis; inserts on the ulnar tuberosity / coronoid process. Forms the floor of the cubital fossa.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: Name and give the origins of the three heads of triceps brachii.
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: Long head (infraglenoid tubercle), lateral head & medial head (both from the humerus). Inserts on the olecranon.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: What extra action does the long head of triceps have at the shoulder?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: It extends and adducts the arm (it crosses the glenohumeral joint).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: Where do the superficial flexors of the forearm share a common origin?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: The common flexor origin — the medial epicondyle of the humerus.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: What is the action of flexor carpi radialis?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: Flexes and abducts the wrist (radial deviation).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: What is the action and nerve of flexor carpi ulnaris?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: Flexes and adducts the wrist; ulnar nerve (the ulnar exception in the superficial layer).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: Which forearm muscle is absent in ~15% of people and is a classic tendon-graft donor?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: Palmaris longus.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: Which joints do FDS and FDP each flex?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: FDS flexes the PIP (middle phalanges); FDP flexes the DIP (distal phalanges).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: Describe the dual nerve supply of flexor digitorum profundus.
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: Lateral half (index & middle) = median nerve via the AIN; medial half (ring & little) = ulnar nerve.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: What is the primary pronator of the forearm and its nerve?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: Pronator quadratus; median nerve (anterior interosseous branch, AIN).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: Which muscles does the anterior interosseous nerve (AIN) supply, and what sign does its palsy give?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: FPL, pronator quadratus & the lateral half of FDP. Palsy → inability to make the “OK” sign (weak thumb–index pinch).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: Where do the superficial extensors of the forearm arise?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: The common extensor origin — the lateral epicondyle of the humerus.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: What is the action of brachioradialis, and what is odd about it?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: Flexes the elbow (strongest in mid-pronation). It is a flexor that sits in the extensor compartment and is radial-supplied.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: Which three muscles make up the “mobile wad”?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: Brachioradialis, extensor carpi radialis longus & extensor carpi radialis brevis.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: The PIN pierces which muscle, and where can it be entrapped?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: The supinator; entrapment occurs at the arcade of Frohse.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: Which muscles form the borders of the anatomical snuffbox?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: Radial border — APL & EPB; ulnar border — EPL.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: How does a PIN lesion differ from a high radial nerve lesion?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: PIN → finger drop with preserved wrist extension (ECRL is spared); high radial → complete wrist drop.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: What does “LOAF” stand for (the median-supplied intrinsics)?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: Lateral two lumbricals, Opponens pollicis, Abductor pollicis brevis, Flexor pollicis brevis.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: What is the nerve of the thenar muscles versus the hypothenar muscles?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: Thenar = recurrent branch of the median nerve; hypothenar = ulnar nerve.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: What is the action and nerve of adductor pollicis, and which clinical sign tests it?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: Adducts the thumb; ulnar nerve (deep branch); tested by Froment’s sign.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: What is the action of the lumbricals and how is their nerve supply split?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: They flex the MCP and extend the IP joints. Lateral 2 = median; medial 2 = ulnar.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.front: What do DAB and PAD tell you about the interossei (and their nerve)?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.back: Dorsal interossei ABduct the fingers (DAB); Palmar interossei ADduct (PAD). All ulnar-supplied.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: From which spinal levels is the brachial plexus formed?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: The anterior rami of C5–T1.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: Name the five stages of the brachial plexus in order (and the mnemonic).
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: Roots → Trunks → Divisions → Cords → Branches (“Randy Travis Drinks Cold Beer”).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: Which two nerves branch directly from the roots of the plexus?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: Dorsal scapular nerve (C5 → rhomboids, levator scapulae) and the long thoracic nerve (C5–C7 → serratus anterior).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: Which nerve arising from the roots supplies serratus anterior?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: The long thoracic nerve (C5–C7).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: What does the dorsal scapular nerve supply?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: The rhomboids and levator scapulae.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: Which two nerves branch from the upper trunk?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: The suprascapular nerve and the nerve to subclavius.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: What does the suprascapular nerve supply?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: Supraspinatus and infraspinatus (motor); it also gives sensory articular branches to the shoulder & acromioclavicular joints (so it is chiefly, not purely, motor).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: Which stage of the brachial plexus gives off no branches?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: The divisions (“no branches come off the divisions”).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: How are the three cords named?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: By their position relative to the axillary artery — lateral, posterior and medial cords.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: List the branches of the lateral cord (“LLM”).
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: Lateral pectoral nerve, lateral root of the median nerve, musculocutaneous nerve.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: List the branches of the medial cord.
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: Medial pectoral nerve, medial cutaneous nerve of arm, medial cutaneous nerve of forearm, ulnar nerve, and the medial root of the median nerve.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: List the branches of the posterior cord (“ULTRA”).
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: Upper subscapular, Lower subscapular, Thoracodorsal, Radial, Axillary.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: What does the thoracodorsal nerve supply?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: Latissimus dorsi.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: What do the upper and lower subscapular nerves supply?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: Upper subscapular → subscapularis; lower subscapular → subscapularis and teres major.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: How is the median nerve formed?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: From a lateral root (lateral cord) and a medial root (medial cord) that unite in front of the axillary artery (the “M” of the plexus).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: Name the five terminal branches of the plexus (“MARMU”).
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: Musculocutaneous, Axillary, Radial, Median, Ulnar.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: Which nerves arise above the cords (a classic exam point)?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: From roots: dorsal scapular & long thoracic. From the upper trunk: suprascapular & nerve to subclavius.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: Give the roots and motor supply of the musculocutaneous nerve.
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: C5–C7; supplies the anterior arm flexors — coracobrachialis, biceps brachii & brachialis.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: The musculocutaneous nerve continues as which cutaneous nerve?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: The lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: Which muscle does the musculocutaneous nerve pierce?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: Coracobrachialis.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: Give the roots and course of the axillary nerve.
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: C5–C6; passes through the quadrangular space and wraps the surgical neck of the humerus (with the posterior circumflex humeral artery).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: What are the motor and sensory supplies of the axillary nerve?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: Motor: deltoid & teres minor. Sensory: the “regimental badge” area over the deltoid (upper lateral cutaneous nerve of arm).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: How many motor branches does the median nerve give in the arm?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: None — the median nerve gives no branches in the arm.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: Through which structure does the median nerve enter the hand?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: The carpal tunnel (deep to the flexor retinaculum).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: What does the anterior interosseous nerve (AIN) supply?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: Flexor pollicis longus, pronator quadratus and the lateral half of FDP (index/middle).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: Why is thenar skin sensation spared in carpal tunnel syndrome?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve leaves proximal to the carpal tunnel, so it is not compressed.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: Where does the ulnar nerve pass at the elbow?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: Behind the medial epicondyle (the cubital tunnel — the “funny bone”).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: Through which structure does the ulnar nerve enter the hand?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: Guyon’s canal (superficial to the flexor retinaculum, between pisiform & hook of hamate).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: Which forearm muscles does the ulnar nerve supply?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: Flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus only.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: Which hand muscles does the ulnar nerve supply?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: All intrinsics except the LOAF muscles — i.e. hypothenar, all interossei, medial 2 lumbricals & adductor pollicis.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: Why is dorsomedial hand sensation preserved in a Guyon’s canal ulnar lesion?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: The dorsal cutaneous branch of the ulnar nerve arises proximal to the wrist, so it escapes a lesion at the canal.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: Describe the course of the radial nerve in the arm.
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: The largest branch of the posterior cord; it spirals down the radial (spiral) groove of the humerus with the profunda brachii artery.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: What is the radial nerve’s motor supply in the arm?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: Triceps brachii (and anconeus).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: Into which two branches does the radial nerve divide at the elbow?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: A superficial (sensory) branch and a deep branch that becomes the posterior interosseous nerve (PIN).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: The PIN pierces which muscle, and at what structure may it be entrapped?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: Supinator; entrapment occurs at the arcade of Frohse.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: Which nerve supplies the skin of the “regimental badge” over the lateral shoulder?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: The axillary nerve (upper lateral cutaneous nerve of arm).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: Which nerve supplies the skin of the lateral forearm?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: The musculocutaneous nerve (via the lateral cutaneous nerve of forearm).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: Which nerve supplies the skin of the medial forearm?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: The medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: Which nerves supply the skin of the medial arm & axilla?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: The medial cutaneous nerve of the arm and the intercostobrachial nerve (T2).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: Which nerve supplies the palmar skin of the lateral 3½ digits?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: The median nerve.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: Which nerve supplies the dorsal skin of the lateral 3½ digits (proximally)?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: The radial nerve (superficial branch).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: Which nerve supplies the skin (palmar & dorsal) of the medial 1½ digits?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: The ulnar nerve.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: Which dermatome corresponds to the thumb?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: C6.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: Which dermatome corresponds to the middle finger?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: C7.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: Which dermatome corresponds to the little finger?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: C8.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: Which dermatome covers the lateral shoulder / regimental badge region?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: C5.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: Distinguish the sensory loss of a peripheral nerve lesion from a root (dermatome) lesion.
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: A peripheral nerve lesion follows the nerve’s cutaneous territory (sharp borders); a root lesion follows a dermatomal strip with myotomal weakness and a lost reflex.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: Give the reflex root values for biceps/brachioradialis and for triceps.
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: Biceps & brachioradialis = C5–C6; triceps = C7.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: What are the three features of Horner’s syndrome?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: Ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis (± enophthalmos) — from interruption of the sympathetic supply to the head.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.front: Wasted hand intrinsics + Horner’s syndrome should make you think of what?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.back: A Pancoast tumour at the lung apex (or a lower-trunk/T1 plexus lesion).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: Which two bones form the pectoral girdle, and what is special about the clavicle?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: Clavicle & scapula. The clavicle is the only bony connection between the upper limb and the axial skeleton (via the sternoclavicular joint).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: How many bones make up the hand?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: 27 — 8 carpals + 5 metacarpals + 14 phalanges.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: When does the clavicle ossify relative to other bones?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: It is the first bone to ossify (~5th week, intramembranous) and one of the last to finish (medial epiphysis fuses ~25 yr).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: What ligament attachments lie on the inferior surface of the clavicle?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: The conoid tubercle & trapezoid line (coracoclavicular ligament) laterally, the subclavian groove (subclavius) centrally, and the impression for the costoclavicular ligament medially.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: What is the commonest site of clavicular fracture?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: The junction of the middle and lateral thirds (medial fragment pulled up by sternocleidomastoid).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: Name the three borders of the scapula.
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: Superior, medial (vertebral) and lateral (axillary) borders.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: Name the three fossae of the scapula.
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: Supraspinous & infraspinous fossae (posterior, split by the spine) and the subscapular fossa (anterior/costal).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: Name the three processes of the scapula.
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: The spine, the acromion and the coracoid process.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: What attaches to the supraglenoid vs the infraglenoid tubercle?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: Supraglenoid tubercle = long head of biceps; infraglenoid tubercle = long head of triceps.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: Which three muscles attach to the coracoid process?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: Pectoralis minor, coracobrachialis and the short head of biceps.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: What passes through the suprascapular notch, and relative to which ligament?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: The suprascapular nerve passes under the transverse scapular ligament (“Army over, Navy under” — the artery goes over).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: Name the proximal landmarks of the humerus.
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: Head, anatomical neck, greater & lesser tubercles, intertubercular (bicipital) groove, and the surgical neck.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: Which nerve is at risk at the surgical neck of the humerus?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: The axillary nerve (and the posterior circumflex humeral artery).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: What runs in the radial (spiral) groove, and which fracture endangers it?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: The radial nerve; a mid-shaft humeral fracture → wrist drop.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: What articulates with the trochlea versus the capitulum of the humerus?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: Trochlea → trochlear notch of the ulna; capitulum → head of the radius.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: Name the distal fossae of the humerus.
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: Coronoid & radial fossae anteriorly; olecranon fossa posteriorly.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: Which nerve lies behind the medial epicondyle of the humerus?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: The ulnar nerve (the “funny bone”).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: Name the key landmarks of the radius.
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: Head, neck, radial tuberosity (biceps), styloid process, dorsal (Lister’s) tubercle, and the ulnar notch.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: Name the key landmarks of the ulna.
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: Olecranon, coronoid process, trochlear notch, radial notch, ulnar tuberosity (brachialis), distal head & styloid process.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: What is the normal relationship of the radial and ulnar styloid processes?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: The radial styloid lies ~1 cm distal to the ulnar styloid — this is lost with a shortened distal radius fracture (e.g. Colles’).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: Does the ulna take part in the wrist joint?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: No — the ulna is separated from the carpus by the articular disc (TFCC); the radius carries the carpus.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: Which muscle attaches to the radial tuberosity, and which to the ulnar tuberosity?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: Radial tuberosity = biceps brachii; ulnar tuberosity = brachialis.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: Name the proximal carpal row (lateral → medial).
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: Scaphoid, Lunate, Triquetrum, Pisiform.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: Name the distal carpal row (lateral → medial).
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: Trapezium, Trapezoid, Capitate, Hamate.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: Which carpal is most commonly fractured, and what is the risk?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: The scaphoid; risk of avascular necrosis of the proximal pole (retrograde supply) — snuffbox tenderness.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: Which carpal bone is most commonly dislocated?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: The lunate (can cause acute carpal tunnel syndrome).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: Which two carpal bones bound Guyon’s canal, and on which sides?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: The pisiform (medial wall) and the hook of the hamate (lateral wall). Roof = palmar carpal ligament; floor = flexor retinaculum/hypothenar muscles.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: Which carpal forms the saddle joint with the thumb metacarpal?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: The trapezium (with the 1st metacarpal → opposition).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: How many phalanges does the thumb have compared with each finger?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: The thumb has 2 (proximal & distal); each finger has 3 (proximal, middle, distal).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: What type of joint is the sternoclavicular joint, and why is it unique?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: A saddle synovial joint (with an articular disc) — the only bony articulation between the upper limb and the axial skeleton.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: What type of joint is the acromioclavicular joint, and what braces it?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: A plane synovial joint; braced by the coracoclavicular ligament (conoid + trapezoid).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: Classify: shoulder, elbow, radioulnar, wrist, thumb CMC, MCP and IP joints.
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: Shoulder = ball-and-socket; elbow & IP = hinge; radioulnar = pivot; wrist = ellipsoid; thumb CMC = saddle; MCP = condyloid.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: What deepens the glenoid cavity, and by roughly how much?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: The fibrocartilaginous glenoid labrum (~50%).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: Where is the glenohumeral joint capsule weakest?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: Inferiorly → dislocations tend to go anterior/inferior.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: Name the static stabilisers of the shoulder.
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: The glenoid labrum, the capsule with its glenohumeral (superior/middle/inferior) & coracohumeral ligaments, and the coraco-acromial arch (prevents superior dislocation).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: Name the dynamic stabilisers of the shoulder.
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: The rotator cuff (SITS) and the long head of biceps tendon.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: What is unusual about the long head of biceps tendon at the shoulder?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: It is intracapsular but extrasynovial — it runs through the joint but is wrapped in a synovial sheath.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: In anterior shoulder dislocation, which nerve must be checked and what two lesions predispose to recurrence?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: The axillary nerve; a Bankart lesion (labral tear) and a Hill–Sachs lesion (posterolateral humeral-head dent).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: Name the two articulations of the elbow joint.
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: Humero-ulnar (trochlea ↔ trochlear notch) and humero-radial (capitulum ↔ radial head).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: Which ligament (and which part) is the main restraint against valgus at the elbow?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: The ulnar (medial) collateral ligament — specifically its anterior band.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: What is the carrying angle, and what alters it?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: ~5–15° of valgus (greater in females); it is reversed to a “gunstock” deformity after a malunited supracondylar fracture.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: What holds the head of the radius at the proximal radioulnar joint?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: The annular ligament — the radial head spins within it against the radial notch of the ulna.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: What lies at the distal radioulnar joint between the ulnar head and the radius?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: The articular disc (part of the triangular fibrocartilage complex, TFCC).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: What movements do the radioulnar joints produce, and what links the two bones?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: Pronation and supination; the radius & ulna are linked by the interosseous membrane.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: What is a “pulled elbow” and how is it reduced?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: Subluxation of the radial head from the annular ligament in a toddler (a pull on the pronated forearm); reduced by supination + flexion.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: Which carpal bones articulate at the radiocarpal (wrist) joint?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: The distal radius + articular disc with the scaphoid, lunate & triquetrum.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: Which hand joint is a common site of osteoarthritis, and what is the sign?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: The 1st carpometacarpal (thumb) saddle joint → “squaring” of the thumb base.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: Which bone ossifies first in the entire body?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: The clavicle (intramembranous, ~5th week).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: What does CRITOE stand for, and at what ages do the centres appear?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: Capitellum, Radial head, Internal (medial) epicondyle, Trochlea, Olecranon, External (lateral) epicondyle — roughly ages 1-3-5-7-9-11.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.front: Why is the CRITOE order clinically important?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.back: It stops you mistaking a normal ossification centre for a fracture on a child’s elbow X-ray — e.g. a visible trochlea with no internal epicondyle suggests an avulsed medial epicondyle trapped in the joint.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.front: At what landmark does the subclavian artery become the axillary artery?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.back: At the lateral border of the 1st rib.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.front: At what landmark does the axillary artery become the brachial artery?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.back: At the lower border of teres major.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.front: Where does the brachial artery divide into the radial and ulnar arteries?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.back: At the neck of the radius, in the cubital fossa.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.front: Name the four branches of the subclavian artery (“VIT C”).
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.back: Vertebral, Internal thoracic, Thyrocervical trunk, Costocervical trunk.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.front: How do the right and left subclavian arteries arise differently?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.back: The right arises from the brachiocephalic trunk; the left arises directly from the arch of the aorta.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.front: What structure divides the axillary artery into its three parts?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.back: Pectoralis minor (the parts give 1, 2 and 3 branches respectively).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.front: What is the single branch of the 1st part of the axillary artery?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.back: The superior thoracic artery.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.front: Name the two branches of the 2nd part of the axillary artery.
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.back: The thoraco-acromial and lateral thoracic arteries.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.front: Name the three branches of the 3rd part of the axillary artery.
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.back: The subscapular (largest) and the anterior & posterior circumflex humeral arteries.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.front: Which axillary branch travels with the axillary nerve through the quadrangular space?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.back: The posterior circumflex humeral artery.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.front: What two branches does the subscapular artery give?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.back: The circumflex scapular (a key scapular-anastomosis collateral) and the thoracodorsal artery.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.front: Give the mnemonic for the axillary artery branches.
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.back: “Screw The Lawyer, Save A Patient” — Superior thoracic; Thoraco-acromial, Lateral thoracic; Subscapular, Anterior & Posterior circumflex humeral.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.front: What is the main branch of the brachial artery, and which nerve does it accompany?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.back: The profunda brachii (deep brachial) artery; it follows the radial nerve in the spiral groove.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.front: Which other named branches does the brachial artery give near the elbow?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.back: The superior and inferior ulnar collateral arteries (part of the elbow anastomosis) and a nutrient artery.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.front: Where is the brachial pulse felt?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.back: Medial to the biceps tendon in the cubital fossa — the site the BP cuff auscultates.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.front: List the contents of the cubital fossa lateral → medial (“TAN”).
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.back: Biceps Tendon, brachial Artery, median Nerve.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.front: What roofs and protects the brachial artery during venepuncture?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.back: The bicipital aponeurosis (separating the median cubital vein from the artery & median nerve beneath).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.front: Where is the radial pulse felt at the wrist?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.back: Lateral to the flexor carpi radialis (FCR) tendon, over the distal radius.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.front: Where does the radial artery run on its way to the hand?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.back: Down the lateral forearm, then across the floor of the anatomical snuffbox onto the dorsum, diving between the heads of the 1st dorsal interosseous.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.front: Which palmar arch does the radial artery chiefly form?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.back: The deep palmar arch (completed by the deep branch of the ulnar artery).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.front: What branch does the ulnar artery give in the proximal forearm?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.back: The common interosseous artery → anterior & posterior interosseous arteries.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.front: Through what does the ulnar artery enter the hand?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.back: Guyon’s canal (superficial to the flexor retinaculum), with the ulnar nerve.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.front: Which palmar arch does the ulnar artery chiefly form?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.back: The superficial palmar arch (completed by the superficial palmar branch of the radial).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.front: Contrast the superficial and deep palmar arches (dominant artery & position).
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.back: Superficial = mainly ulnar, lies distal; deep = mainly radial, lies proximal.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.front: What does Allen’s test assess, and when is it used?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.back: The collateral arterial supply to the hand through the palmar arches — done before radial-artery cannulation (ABG / arterial line).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.front: What is the scapular anastomosis, and why does it matter?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.back: A network around the scapula linking the subclavian (suprascapular & dorsal scapular) to the axillary (circumflex scapular). It provides collateral flow if the axillary artery is blocked between the thyrocervical trunk and the subscapular origin.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.front: Describe the course of the cephalic vein.
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.back: From the lateral dorsal venous network, up the lateral forearm & arm, through the deltopectoral groove, piercing the clavipectoral fascia to join the axillary vein.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.front: Describe the course of the basilic vein.
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.back: From the medial dorsal venous network, up the medial forearm; it pierces the deep fascia at mid-arm and joins the brachial venae comitantes to form the axillary vein.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.front: What is the median cubital vein and why is it clinically important?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.back: A vein crossing the cubital fossa connecting the cephalic to the basilic vein — the standard site for venepuncture and IV access.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.front: What are the deep veins of the upper limb, and where do they ultimately drain?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.back: Paired venae comitantes accompanying the arteries → axillary vein → subclavian vein → brachiocephalic vein.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.front: Name the five groups of axillary lymph nodes.
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.back: Pectoral (anterior), subscapular (posterior), humeral (lateral), central and apical.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.front: Which axillary node group drains most of the upper limb?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.back: The humeral (lateral) group (along the axillary vein).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.front: Which axillary node group drains the anterior chest wall and most of the breast?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.back: The pectoral (anterior) group.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.front: Which axillary node group receives from all the others and drains onward?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.back: The apical group → the subclavian lymph trunk.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.front: How are the axillary nodes divided into surgical levels?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.back: By pectoralis minor: Level I below/lateral, Level II behind, Level III above/medial (apical).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.front: Roughly how much of the breast drains to the axillary nodes?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.back: About 75% (mainly to the pectoral group) — the anatomical basis of axillary spread in breast cancer.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.front: What do the supratrochlear (cubital) nodes drain, and along which vein do they lie?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.back: The medial hand & forearm (little & ring fingers); they lie along the basilic vein above the medial epicondyle.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.front: What is lymphoedema of the arm a classic complication of?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.back: Axillary lymph node clearance (e.g. for breast cancer) — drainage is disrupted and the arm swells.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.front: What do red streaks tracking up the limb toward the axilla indicate?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.back: Lymphangitis — inflamed lymphatic vessels from spreading infection.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.front: What is a sentinel lymph node?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.back: The first node draining a tumour (e.g. the first axillary node from the breast) — biopsied to stage cancer.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.front: The dorsal venous network of the hand gives rise to which two named superficial veins?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatic.back: The cephalic (from its lateral end) and the basilic (from its medial end) veins.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.question: A 30-year-old sustains a spiral fracture of the mid-shaft of the humerus. On examination he cannot extend his wrist or fingers, but elbow flexion and shoulder movement are intact. Which nerve is injured?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.explanation: The radial nerve runs in the spiral groove of the humeral shaft; a mid-shaft fracture injures it, paralysing the wrist and finger extensors → wrist drop. Triceps (a higher branch) is often spared.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.question: A patient dislocates their shoulder anteriorly. Which single examination finding most specifically indicates the associated nerve injury?
options: Clawing of the ring and little fingers
Loss of sensation over the medial forearm
Loss of sensation over the lateral shoulder
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.explanation: Anterior shoulder dislocation (and surgical-neck fractures) endanger the axillary nerve. It supplies sensation to the ‘regimental badge’ area over the deltoid and motor supply to deltoid/teres minor.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.question: A child falls onto an outstretched hand and sustains a supracondylar fracture of the humerus. Which structures are most at risk, and what is the feared late complication?
options: Axillary nerve and posterior circumflex artery; deltoid wasting
Radial nerve and cephalic vein; wrist drop
Median nerve and brachial artery; Volkmann’s ischaemic contracture
Ulnar nerve and ulnar artery; Dupuytren’s contracture
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.explanation: A supracondylar fracture threatens the median nerve (especially the anterior interosseous branch) and the brachial artery. Arterial injury → forearm compartment syndrome → Volkmann’s ischaemic contracture.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.question: A young adult has persistent wrist pain and tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox after a fall. The initial X-ray is reported as normal. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Immediate open reduction and internal fixation
Apply a below-elbow cast for 48 hours only
Immobilise in a thumb spica and re-image in 10–14 days
Reassure and discharge as a wrist sprain
Prescribe analgesia and arrange routine physiotherapy
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.explanation: Snuffbox tenderness is a scaphoid fracture until proven otherwise, and scaphoid fractures are often occult on the first film. Immobilise and re-image (repeat X-ray/MRI) — missing it risks avascular necrosis and non-union.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.question: Why is a proximal-pole scaphoid fracture particularly prone to avascular necrosis?
options: It is supplied only by the ulnar artery
It is bathed in synovial fluid which prevents healing
Its blood supply enters distally and runs retrograde, so a proximal fracture cuts it off
The scaphoid has no blood supply at all
Its blood supply enters proximally and flows distally
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.explanation: The scaphoid’s blood supply enters distally (dorsal carpal branch of the radial artery) and runs retrograde. A proximal-pole fracture therefore starves the proximal fragment, causing avascular necrosis and non-union.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.question: On being asked to make a fist, a patient’s index and middle fingers remain extended while the ring and little fingers curl normally. Which lesion does this indicate?
options: A low ulnar nerve lesion at the wrist
A radial nerve lesion in the axilla
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.explanation: This is the hand of benediction — a high median nerve lesion. The median-supplied flexors to the index and middle fingers are paralysed, so they cannot flex when making a fist, while the ulnar-supplied ring/little fingers curl normally.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.question: A patient has an ulnar nerve laceration. Counter-intuitively, which lesion location produces the MORE pronounced claw hand?
options: A lesion in the brachial plexus
A lesion at the wrist (lower/distal lesion)
A lesion at the elbow (higher lesion)
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.explanation: The ulnar paradox: a distal (wrist) lesion gives a more obvious claw. A higher (elbow) lesion also paralyses the medial half of FDP, so the fingertips cannot flex and the claw is less marked. The claw worsens as a proximal lesion recovers.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.question: A newborn delivered with shoulder dystocia holds the arm adducted, internally rotated, with the elbow extended and forearm pronated — the ‘waiter’s tip’ posture. Which roots are affected?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.explanation: This is Erb’s palsy — an upper trunk (C5–C6) injury from excessive head–shoulder separation. Loss of abductors, external rotators and elbow flexors/supinators produces the waiter’s tip posture.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.question: A patient has weakness of the small muscles of the hand and a claw deformity after a lower brachial plexus (C8–T1) injury. Which additional finding may accompany it?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.explanation: Klumpke’s palsy (C8–T1) can involve the nearby T1 sympathetic fibres, producing an ipsilateral Horner’s syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) in addition to the claw hand.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.question: A patient with carpal tunnel syndrome has paraesthesia of the lateral fingers and thenar wasting, but sensation over the thenar eminence skin is preserved. What explains the spared skin sensation?
options: The skin is supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve
The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve arises before the tunnel and bypasses it
Sensory fibres regenerate faster than motor fibres
The ulnar nerve supplies the thenar skin
The radial nerve supplies the thenar eminence
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.explanation: The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve leaves the main trunk proximal to the flexor retinaculum and runs superficial to it, so it escapes compression in the tunnel — thenar skin sensation is spared even though the thenar muscles waste.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.question: Froment’s sign is positive when a patient flexes the thumb’s interphalangeal joint to grip a piece of paper. Which muscle is weak, and which nerve is affected?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.explanation: Adductor pollicis (ulnar-innervated) is weak, so the patient substitutes flexor pollicis longus (median) — flexing the thumb IP joint — to hold the paper. A positive Froment’s sign indicates ulnar nerve palsy.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.question: Which rotator cuff muscle initiates the first 15° of shoulder abduction and is the most commonly torn?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.explanation: Supraspinatus initiates abduction (0–15°, thereafter deltoid takes over) and is the most commonly torn/impinged cuff muscle. Infraspinatus and teres minor externally rotate; subscapularis internally rotates.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.question: Listing the contents of the cubital fossa from lateral to medial, which sequence is correct?
options: Brachial artery, median nerve, biceps tendon
Biceps tendon, median nerve, brachial artery
Median nerve, brachial artery, biceps tendon
Biceps tendon, brachial artery, median nerve
Radial nerve, brachial artery, ulnar nerve
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.explanation: Lateral to medial the cubital fossa contains the biceps Tendon, brachial Artery and median Nerve (‘TAN’). The median cubital vein lies in the roof and is the usual venepuncture site.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.question: A patient with a forearm injury develops severe pain that is worse on passive finger extension, out of proportion to the injury. Distal pulses are still present. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Arrange an outpatient nerve conduction study
Elevate the limb above the heart and observe overnight
Urgent fasciotomy — do not wait for pulselessness
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.explanation: Pain out of proportion and on passive stretch is the earliest sign of compartment syndrome. Pulselessness is a late sign — waiting for it risks irreversible muscle necrosis (Volkmann’s contracture). Emergency fasciotomy is indicated.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.question: A man wakes after falling asleep with his arm draped over the back of a chair and cannot extend his wrist. Which nerve is affected and what is this called?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.explanation: Prolonged compression of the radial nerve against the humerus (‘Saturday night palsy’) causes wrist drop from paralysis of the wrist/finger extensors, typically with good recovery.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.question: An elderly woman falls onto an outstretched hand and has a distal radius fracture with dorsal angulation, giving a ‘dinner-fork’ deformity. What is this fracture called?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.explanation: A Colles’ fracture is a distal radius fracture with dorsal angulation (‘dinner-fork’ deformity), typically after a FOOSH in the elderly. A Smith’s fracture is the reverse — volar angulation from a fall on a flexed wrist.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.question: Following an axillary lymph node clearance, a patient cannot fully raise the arm above the head and the medial border of the scapula lifts off the chest wall when pushing against a wall. Which nerve was injured?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.explanation: The long thoracic nerve (C5–C7) supplies serratus anterior and is vulnerable during axillary surgery. Its injury causes a winged scapula and loss of full overhead abduction (impaired scapular rotation).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.question: A keen cyclist develops numbness of the little finger and weakness of the hand’s intrinsic muscles after long rides, with sparing of the dorsal ulnar skin. Where is the lesion?
options: Median nerve in the carpal tunnel
Ulnar nerve at the cubital tunnel (elbow)
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Applied / Clinical.explanation: Handlebar pressure compresses the ulnar nerve in Guyon’s canal at the wrist (‘cyclist’s palsy’). Because the dorsal cutaneous branch leaves proximal to the canal, sensation over the dorsal ulnar hand is spared — helping localise the lesion to the wrist.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.question: A footballer cannot initiate abduction of his arm from his side, but once it is passively lifted to ~20° he can continue lifting it. Which structure is most likely torn?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.explanation: Supraspinatus initiates abduction (0–15°); once the deltoid’s range (15–90°) is reached the patient can continue, so a supraspinatus tear presents as difficulty starting abduction.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.question: Which nerve, if injured during axillary surgery, produces a winged scapula?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.explanation: The long thoracic nerve supplies serratus anterior; its loss lets the medial scapular border lift off the chest wall (winging).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.question: Which muscle is the strongest supinator of the forearm when the elbow is flexed?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.explanation: Biceps brachii is the most powerful supinator, especially with the elbow flexed; the supinator muscle acts alone when supination against no resistance is required.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.question: A patient cannot flex the DIP joint of the index finger, but PIP flexion is intact. Which muscle is affected?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.explanation: FDP inserts on the distal phalanx and flexes the DIP; FDS (intact here) flexes the PIP.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.question: Which muscle is the main (workhorse) flexor of the elbow in all forearm positions?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.explanation: Brachialis flexes the elbow in every position and is the workhorse; biceps is chiefly a supinator and brachioradialis acts best in mid-pronation.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.question: All of the following anterior forearm muscles are supplied by the median nerve EXCEPT:
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.explanation: Flexor carpi ulnaris is one of the 1½ ulnar-supplied muscles of the anterior forearm (the other being the medial half of FDP).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.question: Which muscle both flexes and ADDucts (ulnar-deviates) the wrist?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.explanation: FCU flexes and adducts the wrist. FCR flexes and abducts; ECU extends and adducts.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.question: A patient cannot make the “OK” sign — they cannot flex the thumb IP and index DIP to form a circle. Which nerve is affected?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.explanation: The AIN supplies FPL and the lateral half of FDP (to the index); their weakness prevents the pinch needed for the OK sign.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.question: The “mobile wad of three” consists of brachioradialis plus which two muscles?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.explanation: The mobile wad = brachioradialis + extensor carpi radialis longus + extensor carpi radialis brevis, on the lateral forearm.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.question: A positive Froment’s sign (thumb IP flexes when pinching paper) indicates weakness of which muscle?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.explanation: Adductor pollicis (ulnar nerve) is weak, so the patient substitutes FPL (median) — flexing the thumb IP to grip.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.question: Which nerve supplies all intrinsic hand muscles EXCEPT the thenar group and the lateral two lumbricals?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.explanation: The ulnar nerve supplies the hypothenar muscles, all interossei, the medial two lumbricals and adductor pollicis; the median supplies the LOAF muscles.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.question: The dorsal interossei of the hand perform which primary action?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.explanation: “DAB” — Dorsal interossei ABduct the fingers away from the middle-finger axis. Palmar interossei adduct (PAD).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.question: After a posterior interosseous nerve palsy a patient has finger drop, yet can still extend the wrist (with radial deviation). Why is some wrist extension preserved?
options: Extensor carpi radialis longus is supplied before the PIN branches
The ulnar nerve extends the wrist
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.explanation: ECRL is supplied by the radial nerve proper, proximal to the PIN; it is spared, so the wrist still extends but deviates radially (unopposed ECU loss).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the rotator cuff muscles?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.explanation: Teres major (lower subscapular nerve) is not a cuff muscle; the cuff is SITS — supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.question: For abduction above 90°, the scapula is upwardly rotated by trapezius together with which muscle?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.explanation: Trapezius (upper + lower) and serratus anterior form the force couple that upwardly rotates the scapula to lift the arm overhead.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.question: Which rotator cuff muscle medially rotates the arm?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.explanation: Subscapularis, the anterior cuff muscle, medially rotates; infraspinatus and teres minor laterally rotate.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.question: From where does the long head of biceps brachii originate?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.explanation: The long head arises from the supraglenoid tubercle (short head from the coracoid process); the infraglenoid tubercle gives origin to the long head of triceps.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.question: Which nerve supplies latissimus dorsi?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.explanation: Latissimus dorsi is supplied by the thoracodorsal nerve (a branch of the posterior cord).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.question: A patient who has been walking on axillary crutches develops weak elbow extension together with wrist drop. Which muscle and nerve are involved?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.explanation: A proximal (axillary) radial nerve lesion — classic “crutch palsy” — is above the branches to triceps, so it weakens elbow extension as well as causing wrist drop. (A mid-shaft/spiral-groove lesion usually spares triceps, giving wrist drop alone.)

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.question: Which muscle is the primary pronator of the forearm?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.explanation: Pronator quadratus (AIN) is the primary pronator; pronator teres assists, especially during rapid/forceful pronation.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.question: The common flexor origin of the superficial forearm flexors is located at the:
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.explanation: The superficial flexor-pronator muscles arise from the medial epicondyle; the extensors arise from the lateral epicondyle (common extensor origin).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.question: Which muscle flexes the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints of the fingers?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.explanation: FDS inserts on the middle phalanges and flexes the PIP; FDP flexes the DIP.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.question: Which action best describes the lumbricals?
options: Flex MCP and extend IP joints
Extend MCP and flex IP joints
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Muscles & Movements.explanation: The lumbricals flex the metacarpophalangeal joints while extending the interphalangeal joints (they pass volar to the MCP axis and dorsal to the IP axis).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.question: Which nerve arises from the roots of the brachial plexus and, if injured, produces a winged scapula?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.explanation: The long thoracic nerve (C5–C7) arises from the roots and supplies serratus anterior; its loss causes scapular winging.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.question: The cords of the brachial plexus are named according to their relationship to which structure?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.explanation: Lateral, posterior and medial cords are named by their position around the axillary artery.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.question: Which of the following is a branch of the posterior cord?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.explanation: The posterior cord gives the ULTRA branches: upper subscapular, lower subscapular, thoracodorsal, radial and axillary.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.question: From which part of the brachial plexus does the suprascapular nerve arise?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.explanation: The suprascapular nerve (with the nerve to subclavius) branches from the upper trunk.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.question: A patient cannot flex the elbow or supinate the forearm and has lost sensation over the lateral forearm. Which nerve is injured?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.explanation: The musculocutaneous nerve supplies the anterior-arm flexors and continues as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.question: Which nerve passes through the quadrangular space with the posterior circumflex humeral artery?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.explanation: The axillary nerve (C5–C6) traverses the quadrangular space with the posterior circumflex humeral artery.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.question: How many motor branches does the median nerve give off in the arm?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.explanation: The median nerve gives no branches in the arm; its first branches (including the AIN) arise around the elbow/forearm.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.question: The anterior interosseous nerve is a branch of which nerve?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.explanation: The AIN is the main motor branch of the median nerve in the forearm (FPL, pronator quadratus, lateral FDP).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.question: In carpal tunnel syndrome the skin over the thenar eminence retains normal sensation. Why?
options: The palmar cutaneous branch leaves proximal to the tunnel
The recurrent motor branch carries sensation
The thenar skin has no innervation
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.explanation: The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve arises before the carpal tunnel, so it is not compressed within it.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.question: Through which structure does the ulnar nerve enter the hand?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.explanation: The ulnar nerve enters the hand via Guyon's canal, superficial to the flexor retinaculum.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.question: The deep branch of the radial nerve (PIN) passes through which muscle?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.explanation: The PIN pierces the supinator (at the arcade of Frohse) to reach the extensor compartment.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.question: Which region of skin is supplied by the axillary nerve?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.explanation: The axillary nerve's upper lateral cutaneous nerve of arm supplies the 'regimental badge' area over the deltoid.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.question: The thumb lies within which dermatome?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.explanation: Thumb = C6 (middle finger C7, little finger C8 — count 6-7-8 across the hand).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.question: The middle finger lies within which dermatome?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.explanation: Middle finger = C7.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.question: A patient has weak elbow flexion, a diminished biceps jerk and numbness of the thumb. Which nerve root is affected?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.explanation: Thumb sensation = C6 and the biceps/brachioradialis reflex = C5–C6, so a C6 radiculopathy fits best.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.question: Which deep tendon reflex principally tests the C7 root?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.explanation: The triceps reflex tests C7 (biceps & brachioradialis test C5–C6).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.question: A patient presents with wasting of the small muscles of the hand together with ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis. What is the most likely underlying cause?
options: Pancoast tumour of the lung apex
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.explanation: Lower-plexus (T1) involvement plus Horner's syndrome (ptosis/miosis/anhidrosis) points to a Pancoast apical lung tumour.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.question: Which nerve supplies the skin over the dorsum of the lateral 3½ digits (proximal to the nail beds)?
options: Superficial branch of the radial nerve
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.explanation: The superficial (sensory) branch of the radial nerve supplies the dorsolateral hand; the median supplies the volar surface and the dorsal fingertips.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.question: The ulnar nerve is a terminal branch of which cord?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.explanation: The ulnar nerve arises from the medial cord (C8–T1); the median nerve receives a root from the medial cord as well.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.question: Which nerve is most at risk with a fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.explanation: The axillary nerve curves around the surgical neck and is endangered there (and in anterior shoulder dislocation).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.question: An upper trunk (C5–C6) traction injury of the plexus produces which characteristic posture?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.explanation: Loss of the C5–C6 (upper trunk) muscles gives the adducted, internally rotated, pronated 'waiter's tip' posture of Erb's palsy.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.question: The intercostobrachial nerve (T2) supplies the skin of which region?
options: The medial upper arm and axilla
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.explanation: The intercostobrachial nerve (lateral cutaneous branch of T2) supplies the medial upper arm and floor of the axilla — often injured in axillary clearance.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.question: Which nerve continues distally as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.explanation: After supplying the anterior-arm flexors, the musculocutaneous nerve emerges lateral to the biceps tendon as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.question: Which two nerves branch directly from the roots of the brachial plexus?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Nerves.explanation: The dorsal scapular (C5) and long thoracic (C5–C7) nerves arise from the roots; the suprascapular and nerve to subclavius come off the upper trunk.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.question: Which is the only bony joint connecting the upper limb to the axial skeleton?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.explanation: The sternoclavicular joint (clavicle to manubrium) is the sole bony link between the appendicular upper limb and the axial skeleton.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.question: The long head of biceps brachii arises from which landmark?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.explanation: The long head of biceps arises from the supraglenoid tubercle of the scapula (the infraglenoid tubercle gives the long head of triceps).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.question: Which nerve is most at risk with a fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.explanation: The axillary nerve wraps the surgical neck (with the posterior circumflex humeral artery) and is endangered there.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.question: A patient falls onto the outstretched hand and has tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox. Which carpal bone is most likely fractured?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.explanation: Snuffbox tenderness after a FOOSH indicates a scaphoid fracture until proven otherwise; its retrograde blood supply risks proximal-pole AVN.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.question: Which carpal bone is most commonly dislocated and may cause acute carpal tunnel syndrome?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.explanation: The lunate is the most commonly dislocated carpal; anterior dislocation can compress the median nerve, causing acute CTS.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.question: The carpometacarpal joint of the thumb is which type of synovial joint?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.explanation: The 1st CMC joint (trapezium–MC1) is a saddle joint, allowing opposition; it is a common site of osteoarthritis.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.question: Which structure deepens the shallow glenoid cavity?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.explanation: The fibrocartilaginous glenoid labrum deepens the glenoid by roughly 50%, improving stability.

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.question: In which direction does the glenohumeral joint most commonly dislocate?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.explanation: The capsule is weakest inferiorly, so dislocations typically pass anteroinferiorly (arm abducted + externally rotated).

anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.question: Which ligament encircles and retains the head of the radius?
anatomy__UPPER LIMB__Osteology & Joints.explanation: The annular ligament wraps the radial head against the radial notch of the ulna at the proximal radioulnar joint.
